title: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tools
gist: The UK borders watchdog ICIBI is weighing an inspection of the Home Office's GPT-4-based asylum tools (ACS and APS, built with Microsoft Foundry), after Open Rights Group found error rates above the published 9% and no quality control on policy summaries. The tools save about an hour per case amid a 100,000-case backlog push, but are missing from the government's public algorithm register, and the data regulator is already investigating.

insights.claim: The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI) is considering an investigation into the UK Home Office's use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications and has asked Open Rights Group for information as it sets next year's inspection priorities.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Government AI deployments face growing oversight risk that can slow public-sector AI procurement.
insights.locator: The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders

insights.claim: The UK's Information Commission is investigating the Home Office's refusal to tell Open Rights Group how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Data-protection regulators are becoming active enforcers on government AI transparency.
insights.locator: Both groups have sent their findings

insights.claim: Lawyers at Cloisters, in an opinion commissioned by Open Rights Group, argue that asylum seekers' inability to contest incorrect AI summaries of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Contestability requirements could impose legal liability and design constraints on AI in decision-making.
insights.locator: Asylum seekers are also not told

insights.claim: Despite the UK 'AI Playbook' requiring departments to list algorithmic decision tools on a public repository, the Home Office's ACS and APS tools are not listed, and the Public Law Project has found 11 high-risk AI systems used across government that are absent from the repository.
insights.speaker: Caroline Selman
insights.so_what: Undisclosed government AI usage is widespread, inviting tighter transparency rules for vendors and agencies.
insights.quote: you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.
insights.locator: Public Law Project senior research fellow

themes.theme: OpenAI and Microsoft in government workflows

insights.claim: The Home Office's Asylum Case Summarisation and Asylum Policy Search tools are built on OpenAI's 2023 GPT-4 model and Microsoft Foundry, and were piloted from late 2024 to help clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: OpenAI and Microsoft are embedded in sensitive government workflows, bringing both revenue and reputational risk.

insights.claim: Government estimates show the two tools used together saved around an hour per asylum case in the pilot.

insights.so_what: Quantified productivity gains underpin the public-sector business case for LLM adoption.

insights.claim: OpenAI will retire GPT-4 in January, while the Home Office's asylum tools still run on it.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Model deprecation forces government customers into migrations and revalidation, a hidden cost of LLM deployments.

insights.claim: The Home Office halved the number of people waiting on an initial asylum decision in the year through June, but appeals against decisions have ballooned.

insights.claim: Open Rights Group found the share of Asylum Case Summarisation outputs deemed unfit for use, often due to factual errors, is significantly higher than the 9 percent error rate published in the pilot evaluation, and there is no quality control on Asylum Policy Search summaries.

insights.so_what: Real-world LLM error rates exceeding pilot figures undermine vendor accuracy claims in high-stakes uses.
